item.title: Israel votes Tuesday
item.description:
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu faces a fight for political survival, Reuters reports, with voters weighing his leadership after the 2023 Hamas-led attacks and the wars in Gaza and with Iran.
Polls show a close race between Netanyahu's Likud and its right-wing allies and a rival alliance led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot. Netanyahu is campaigning on his wartime leadership and his alliance with President Trump, who has endorsed him; Eisenkot accuses Netanyahu of "fear-mongering, lies and threats" and says Trump would work with any leader chosen by voters.
Neither side has a clear path to a governing coalition in the 120-seat parliament, Reuters notes — if neither can form one, Netanyahu could stay on as caretaker until another election next year. Polls open 7 a.m. to 10 p.m. local time Tuesday.
Source:
Source: 935thelloyd.com.

item.title: CISA adds two critical PHP flaws to its exploited list — federal deadline October 29
item.description:
CISA added CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on October 26, SSJ News reports.
Both are unauthenticated remote-code-execution flaws in PHP's web-serving configurations, rated CVSS 9.2, with fixed releases PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35 (PHP 8.1 and earlier get no patches). CISA's updated alert directs organizations that cannot update immediately, or still run unsupported versions, to take PHP-based systems offline until they can be patched.
This escalates the PHP2Shell flaws already reported Monday morning from "reported exploited" to formally listed as exploited with a federal deadline. Source:
Source: ssj.news.

item.title: State Bank of India breach disclosed
item.description:
India's state-run State Bank of India, serving more than 500 million customers, disclosed a data breach after 3,897 customer records appeared online, Check Point Research reports in its October 26 threat report.
Exposed information reportedly included contact details, residential addresses, birth dates, bank profiles, loan records and identity-verification documents. The bank reported no disruption to core services.
Source:
Source: research.checkpoint.com.

item.title: Talks in Tehran, troops on standby in Cairo: the region tries diplomacy while the attacks continue
item.description:
Top officials from Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan met Iran's leaders in Tehran on Monday in the first high-level contact between Iran and all three Mecca Pact countries since the war spread to Saudi Arabia and Yemen. By the end of the day, Reuters reports, the four states had agreed to keep talking, with a view to strengthening cooperation on peace and security. On the same day, Egypt's parliament authorized its military to help defend Saudi Arabia if Riyadh asks — a move that could pull the Arab world's most populous country directly into the conflict. And on the same day, the Houthis said they had attacked pumping stations on Saudi Arabia's East-West oil pipeline as well as Riyadh's airport. There was no immediate Saudi confirmation of those claims.
The Tehran meeting was heavyweight. Saudi Arabia was represented by Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman, Pakistan by army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir, and Turkey by intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin, meeting Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi and Supreme National Security Council secretary Mohsen Rezaei. The Saudi Foreign Ministry said the visit was meant to open negotiating channels to "prevent the return of military escalation." A senior Pakistani security official told Reuters the focus was building a regional non-aggression network, and another Pakistani official said Munir — with what the official described as a go-ahead from Trump to try diplomacy — had presented Iran with a proposal meant to offer something to both Washington and Tehran, with the Mecca Pact states and Qatar as possible guarantors if it is accepted. No details of the proposal were given.
The two sides are still far apart on what a deal even covers. An Iranian official said there would be no discussion of Iran's nuclear programme at Monday's meeting until Tehran's demands for ending the war are met — ending a US blockade of Iranian ports and lifting sanctions on Iranian oil exports, according to Reuters. US Vice President JD Vance, by contrast, has said Iran must reduce nuclear enrichment to end the war. Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei framed Monday's agenda more broadly: "Israel's expansionist policies, developments in the Palestinian territories and Lebanon, and the repercussions of US and Israeli military action against Iran." Meanwhile the threat picture behind the talks has not softened: Trump said Friday the US may carry out another military operation against Iran, Iranian security officials told Reuters Tehran has drawn up plans to attack Gulf undersea cables if the US and Israel attack again, and the New York Times, citing senior US officials, reported Trump is privately leaning toward another round of strikes, with US Central Command drawing up an expanded target list including Iran's energy infrastructure.
Egypt's authorization is the day's second big shift, and it comes with limits worth noting. Parliament voted in closed session, with at least two-thirds backing the measure according to an official statement, authorizing President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi to take "all necessary measures" to help Saudi Arabia defend itself. But no formal Saudi request for Egyptian troops has been announced, the statement did not specify what kind of support Egypt would provide, and opposition groups objected or abstained — the Civil Democratic Movement rejected Egyptian military involvement in a regional war, and the Egyptian Social Democratic Party abstained, citing a lack of information on the mission's aims, duration and cost. Egypt has condemned Iranian-backed attacks for months but has not publicly fought in this war and has not joined the Mecca Pact; its foreign minister said this month that membership remains "under serious consideration." One unnamed regional official told the Associated Press the support under discussion involved aircraft and air defences, not ground troops in Yemen — unconfirmed, and no deployment has been announced.
For ordinary people, the war's costs are still measured in fuel prices and shipping, not in communiqués. Brent crude fell on Monday — down about $1.90 to roughly $115–116 a barrel, with WTI around $101–102 — as traders priced in the diplomacy, but both benchmarks remain near six-month highs after a 6% weekly gain for Brent. Only eight vessels transited the Strait of Hormuz in the last 24 hours, according to vessel tracking cited by DTN, against a normal daily average of nearly sixty, and about 500 commercial vessels are reported waiting outside the passage for convoy slots or refusing transit over insurance costs. The Houthi claims matter here even unconfirmed: the East-West pipeline is Saudi Arabia's overland bypass around Hormuz, and the Houthis already claimed strikes on it, the Yanbu terminal and the Rabigh refinery over the weekend. If the bypass itself is a target, there is less slack in the system for everyone buying fuel.
In short: Monday produced a real diplomatic channel — four states in one room in Tehran, agreeing to keep talking, with a Pakistani proposal on the table — and, in parallel, a real military authorization in Cairo and fresh Houthi claims on Saudi oil infrastructure. Neither cancels the other. Watch whether the Tehran channel produces anything concrete before the November 3 midterms, and whether Riyadh actually calls on Egypt's authorization.
Sources:
Source: devdiscourse.com.

item.title: What Tuesday's ceasefire is actually for
item.description:
Russia and Ukraine agreed on October 23 to a local ceasefire around the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky in southern Ukraine, starting October 27, to allow aid deliveries and evacuations through humanitarian corridors.
Reuters' Monday explainer adds the human scale the morning brief didn't: Oleshky sits on the eastern bank of the Dnipro, opposite Ukrainian-held Kherson city, has been occupied since the first days of the February 2022 invasion, was hit hard by flooding after the Kakhovka dam destruction in 2023, and now holds only a few thousand people from a prewar population of 24,000, with severe shortages of food and medicine. The White House says First Lady Melania Trump helped broker the deal, with involvement from Pope Leo.
Whether aid actually moves on Tuesday is the test — both sides were already accusing each other of striking the town before the ceasefire starts. Source:
Source: 935thelloyd.com.

item.title: Apple opens its product week with the OLED iPad mini — its biggest update ever, and its second price hike this year
item.description:
Apple on Monday announced the all-new iPad mini, its first with an OLED display — the product Bloomberg's Mark Gurman had tipped to lead a three-day announcement run, and the first confirmed launch of the week ahead of Wednesday's "Pro and tell" event. The new mini has a larger 8.5-inch Super Retina XDR OLED display (up from 8.3-inch LCD, with 24% thinner bezels, up to 1,200 nits peak brightness and a 2,000,000:1 contrast ratio), Apple's A20 Pro chip, a 5.4mm-thin design, IP67 water and dust resistance, a new Acoustic Display speaker system, a 12MP Center Stage front camera on the landscape edge, Apple's N1 wireless chip (Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6, Thread) and the C2 modem on cellular models, running iPadOS 27 with the new Siri AI. Apple calls it the biggest update ever to the iPad mini, and on the hardware that is hard to dispute: the A20 Pro claims up to 4.5x faster AI performance, 2.7x faster graphics and 60% faster multithreaded performance than the previous A17 Pro model.
The other side of the story is the price, and it is the part buyers will actually feel. The new mini starts at $699 for 128GB Wi-Fi ($849 cellular), up $100 from the $599 the previous model was raised to earlier this year — and $200 more than the $499 launch price of the A17 Pro mini in 2024. Storage tiers run 128GB/256GB/512GB ($699/$799/$899 Wi-Fi, per Pocket-lint), with a $100 nano-texture glass option on the larger tiers, and the new TechWoven Smart Folio costs $79, up from $59. The colour range also narrowed from four finishes to two: Midnight and Starlight. And one widely expected spec did not arrive: Pocket-lint notes the display is still 60Hz — no ProMotion — which stings more at $699, close to iPad Air territory. Pre-orders open Wednesday, October 28, with availability Friday, November 6, in 36 countries. Apple marketing chief Greg Joswiak teased that the mini is "only the start" of an exciting week, and Gurman expects M6 iMac and MacBook Pro announcements on Tuesday, ahead of the touchscreen MacBook Pro reveal on Wednesday.
For ordinary buyers, the math is simple: this is a genuinely much better small tablet — OLED, faster chip, water resistance, better audio — that now costs what a small tablet with those specs arguably should, but $200 more than the same device's launch price two years ago, in a year of sweeping Apple price increases blamed on memory and chip shortages. If you already own the A17 Pro mini, the OLED screen and water resistance are the reasons to upgrade; the chip alone probably is not.
In short: Apple's week started with a real launch, not a rumour — the OLED iPad mini is here, it is a major upgrade, and it costs $699. The question for Tuesday is whether the M6 Macs follow on schedule, and for Wednesday whether the touchscreen MacBook Pro lives up to its billing.
Sources:
Source: apple.com.

Apple calls it the biggest update ever to the iPad mini, and on the hardware that is hard to dispute: the A20 Pro claims up to 4.5x faster AI performance, 2.7x faster graphics and 60% faster multithreaded performance than the previous A17 Pro model.

The other side of the story is the price, and it is the part buyers will actually feel. The new mini starts at $699 for 128GB Wi-Fi ($849 cellular), up $100 from the $599 the previous model was raised to earlier this year — and $200 more than the $499 launch price of the A17 Pro mini in 2024. Storage tiers run 128GB/256GB/512GB ($699/$799/$899 Wi-Fi, per Pocket-lint), with a $100 nano-texture glass option on the larger tiers, and the new TechWoven Smart Folio costs $79, up from $59. The colour range also narrowed from four finishes to two: Midnight and Starlight. And one widely expected spec did not arrive: Pocket-lint notes the display is still 60Hz — no ProMotion — which stings more at $699, close to iPad Air territory. Pre-orders open Wednesday, October 28, with availability Friday, November 6, in 36 countries. Apple marketing chief Greg Joswiak teased that the mini is "only the start" of an exciting week, and Gurman expects M6 iMac and MacBook Pro announcements on Tuesday, ahead of the touchscreen MacBook Pro reveal on Wednesday.

For ordinary buyers, the math is simple: this is a genuinely much better small tablet — OLED, faster chip, water resistance, better audio — that now costs what a small tablet with those specs arguably should, but $200 more than the same device's launch price two years ago, in a year of sweeping Apple price increases blamed on memory and chip shortages. If you already own the A17 Pro mini, the OLED screen and water resistance are the reasons to upgrade; the chip alone probably is not.

In short: Apple's week started with a real launch, not a rumour — the OLED iPad mini is here, it is a major upgrade, and it costs $699. The question for Tuesday is whether the M6 Macs follow on schedule, and for Wednesday whether the touchscreen MacBook Pro lives up to its billing.

item.title: Google open-sources Elephant-Goldfish (EGM) — design-first AI coding, Apache 2.0
item.description:
Google's Elephant-Goldfish Model, now on GitHub, forces a design review before any code is generated: the "Elephant" holds the project's long-term memory and turns architecture discussions into a design document, then stateless "Goldfish" reviewers read the plan cold, hunting for ambiguity, missing assumptions and edge cases.
Nothing gets implemented until the plan survives review and the human approves it. Google says thousands of its own engineers already use it for production software, though it has published no public benchmarks on speed or quality.
Worth a try if one-shot code generation keeps handing you confident nonsense. Source:
Source: en.softonic.com.

item.description:
The Brotli decoder bundled with Node.js 26.x, 24.x and 22.x has an out-of-bounds write (CVSS 9.2 from Google as CNA) that can corrupt process memory via attacker-controlled compressed data, potentially crashing the process, leaking memory or enabling remote code execution.
No exploitation in the wild known as of October 26 and not in CISA KEV — but Rapid7 recommends prioritizing remediation for apps that decompress attacker-supplied data. Source:
Source: rapid7.com.

item.title: "Decision time" on Iran: Trump weighs a deal or a new bombing campaign, as mediators work Tehran
item.description:
President Donald Trump said Sunday it is "getting to be decision time" on Iran: make a deal, or "finish it off." In an interview with Fox News' "Sunday Morning Futures," he put it in his own terms, as Bloomberg reported: "I have a decision to make: Do I finish it off, which would be very easy to do, or do I make a deal? That's all. We don't play games." Later Sunday, leaving the White House, he told reporters there would be no strike that day — a one-day ruling-out, not a decision, and the same line he gave the previous night.
Washington's side of the argument is that the earlier campaign did not settle the question permanently, and that the threat picture is getting worse. Bloomberg reports Trump has suggested US strikes could resume after the November 3 midterm elections and has sent additional forces, including a third aircraft carrier group, toward the Persian Gulf. US officials warn the stretch between the election and the new Congress taking office could be especially dangerous, with a negotiated deal seen as the most likely way to end the conflict. The US is also reducing diplomatic and military staffing in parts of the Middle East, Bloomberg reports, as Iran intensifies attacks on ships near the Strait of Hormuz and Houthi threats against Americans grow. An American official told Bloomberg on Friday that staffing changes go beyond Saudi Arabia, where departures were first acknowledged.
Tehran's side, as described by people familiar with its thinking, is that it is bracing for a fresh bombing campaign around the midterms and preparing to retaliate across the Middle East, including against Israel and the United Arab Emirates. Iran is also now attacking more ships in or near the Strait of Hormuz — and causing more severe damage — than earlier in the conflict, deploying guided missiles rather than attack drones, according to shipping and maritime security officials cited by Bloomberg. "All indications point to a resumption of war and a major bombing campaign, although the timing remains uncertain," Aslı Aydıntaşbaş, a Middle East expert at the Brookings Institution, told Bloomberg. Iran's own public line, repeated through the weekend, is that renewed attacks would not change its positions and would not produce a different outcome from previous operations.
The diplomacy is real but narrow. Qatari mediators travelled to Tehran on Sunday as part of a US-coordinated effort to ease tensions, Reuters reported, and on Monday top officials from the Mecca Pact countries — Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan — are set to meet Iran's leaders in Tehran, their first high-level contact since Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia became a pressure point in the wider conflict. Israel adds its own clock: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth made an unannounced stop in Israel to meet Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu just days ahead of Israel's election on Tuesday, the first since the Hamas attacks in 2023. Bloomberg notes that if Netanyahu loses, his chief rival, Gadi Eisenkot, may not be as eager to begin his term restarting the Iran war.
For ordinary people, the immediate effect showed up at the pump and on the markets rather than in a new strike. Brent crude fell 1.63% to $114.82 a barrel and US West Texas Intermediate fell 2% to $101.19 by mid-morning GMT on Monday, Reuters reported, after Brent gained about 6% last week — but both remain near six-month highs, and analysts warned the calm may be temporary. "With the jeopardy doubled by Houthi attacks into Saudi, any Brent price dips back to the lows of last week will find grateful buyers," PVM Oil Associates analyst John Evans told Reuters. Gulf residents still face airport alerts, rerouted flights and the standing US travel advisories for the region.
In short: no strike Sunday, no deal announced, and no decision taken — but the decision window is now explicitly framed as deal-or-bombing, with mediators in Tehran on Monday, a third carrier group moving, and Washington's own assessment pointing past the November 3 midterms. Watch the Mecca Pact meeting in Tehran today and Israel's election on Tuesday for the next shift.
Sources:
Source: moneyweb.co.za.

item.title: Riyadh's skies, by the numbers: 86% of flights cancelled this month, and the airport's partial reopening met a fresh Houthi claim
item.description:
The Houthi campaign against Saudi aviation now has a full-month tally, and it is stark. About 86% of scheduled flights at Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport — 4,071 out of 4,736 — were cancelled between October 8 and October 25, according to aviation analytics firm Cirium, as Reuters reported Monday. Across all Saudi airports, more than 7,800 flights, or 45% of scheduled departures, were cancelled in the same period, peaking on October 12, when cancellations exceeded 60% nationwide. Dammam saw 42% cancelled and Abha 46.7%, while Najran, near the Yemeni border, had all flights cancelled.
Saudi authorities partially reopened Riyadh's airport on Sunday after a halt that began on October 10, when an attack killed 13 people — the deadliest in the kingdom in more than a decade. Domestic flights resumed from Terminal 1, while national carriers were allowed to operate international services from Terminal 2. But the reopening did not hold the news cycle for a day: the Houthis said they had attacked Riyadh's airport again on Monday, calling it a "military target." Reuters could not independently confirm damage from the Monday claim, and Saudi authorities have not confirmed a successful strike on the airport in the latest claim — a gap worth keeping in mind, since Houthi claims and confirmed impacts have diverged before.
The two sides are arguing past each other in familiar terms. The Houthis present airports, ports and oil facilities as legitimate targets and retaliation for Saudi airstrikes on Yemen, including strikes on Sanaa and other areas over the weekend that they cite for the latest attacks. Riyadh's position, shown in its actions rather than a single statement, is to keep the airport running where it can — partial reopening, domestic first — while intercepting incoming missiles and drones, as it said it did repeatedly over the weekend. The airlines are voting with their schedules: international carriers have suspended services to the Saudi capital into November, Delta Air Lines has postponed the launch of its Riyadh route until next year, and several events in Riyadh have been cancelled or postponed, including Saudi Arabia's marquee investment conference.
For ordinary people, this is the war arriving as a cancelled flight, a postponed conference, and a longer, more expensive route around the Gulf. Riyadh's airport is the kingdom's second-busiest after Jeddah, and the disruption has spread well beyond the capital — nearly half of all Saudi departures gone for more than two weeks is a national transport shutdown in all but name, even with Sunday's partial reopening.
In short: the numbers confirm what travellers already felt — Riyadh's airport has been operating at a fraction of normal all month, the partial reopening is real but fragile, and the Houthis are already claiming to have tested it on its first full day back. Watch whether international carriers extend their suspensions past November, and whether the Terminal 1/2 reopening survives the week.
Sources:
Source: wncy.com.

item.title: Ukraine: overnight strikes hit power plants and a port again, while a slow eastern push pulls Russian marines off the attack
item.description:
Russian strikes overnight hit Ukrainian cities and infrastructure again, while the front line in the east moved — slowly, but in Ukraine's favour, according to the Institute for the Study of War. A Russian strike on the southeastern city of Zaporizhzhia injured four people overnight, regional governor Mykhailo Semikin said on Telegram on Monday, Reuters reported, and two more people were injured in strikes on the Chernihiv region. Russia's defence ministry said on Telegram that it hit a power station in Kharkiv, a warehouse in the surrounding region, and another power station in the Khmelnitskiy region, plus port infrastructure in Chornomorsk and a cargo vessel en route to Odesa that it said was used for military purposes. Reuters could not independently verify the ministry's claims of what was hit, and the Ukrainian side's account centres on the civilian injuries and the power targets.
The political argument around the strikes sharpened in a Sunday interview with President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. He said Kyiv would halt its strikes on Russian oil refineries only if Moscow stops hitting Ukrainian power infrastructure — or, alternatively, if the United States allows the use of Starshield over Russia to detect missile launch sites, or supplies Ukraine with Patriot missiles. The US, Reuters noted, has pressed Ukraine to suspend the refinery strikes, arguing they add to high energy prices — a sensitive issue for the Trump administration amid its war on Iran and with midterm elections approaching next month. Zelenskyy's framing turns the American ask into a trade: stop the refinery campaign in exchange for either Russian restraint on the grid or the tools to defend it. Moscow has not publicly accepted either version.
On the ground, ISW's October 25 assessment reports Ukrainian forces retook three settlements near Oleksandrivka — Perebudova, Komar and Fedorivka — and advanced toward Skudne, likely pushing Russian troops out of a salient northwest of the Fedorivka-Burlatske line, though Russian forces still hold the northeastern edge of Perebudova. The pressure has already changed Russian deployments, ISW says: elements of the Baltic Fleet's 120th Naval Infantry Division and the Pacific Fleet's 40th Separate Naval Infantry Brigade were redeployed to defend the Oleksandrivka direction instead of supporting offensives toward Hulyaipole, and elements of the 90th Tank Division earmarked for Druzhkivka were also pulled in. Those are among Russia's more combat-capable formations, ISW notes, and using them defensively is a sign of strain. Elsewhere the picture is mixed — Russian forces recently advanced in the Novopavlivka direction, southwest of Filiya — and Ukraine's jet-powered drone interception rate slipped from about 77% to about 74% during the October 14–24 Starshield disruption period, though ISW also notes Ukrainian officials confirmed unrestricted Starlink and Starshield access resumed on October 24.
A third thread could matter more for civilians than either front line: the local ceasefire in Oleshky. Ukraine and Russia agreed on Friday that a ceasefire in the Russian-controlled town in Kherson Oblast would take effect on October 27, allowing aid deliveries and evacuations through humanitarian corridors. On Monday, Russia's defence ministry accused Ukraine of striking the town 18 times with artillery and carrying out more than 120 drone attacks on it and nearby roads since October 19, saying this thwarted food and medicine deliveries and stopped people leaving. Reuters could not independently verify that claim, and there was no immediate response from Ukraine, which has in the past accused Russia of not letting aid in or people out. Treat the accusation as unverified — but the ceasefire itself starts Tuesday, and whether aid actually moves will be the test.
For ordinary Ukrainians, the pattern is unchanged and grinding: power stations as targets as winter approaches, port infrastructure under threat at Chornomorsk, and a rare local ceasefire that could, if it holds, let civilians in one occupied town get food, medicine and a way out.
In short: another night of strikes on the grid and the ports, a Ukrainian advance in the east that is forcing Russia to spend its better units on defence, and an Oleshky ceasefire due Tuesday that both sides are already arguing about before it starts. Watch Tuesday for whether aid moves in Oleshky, and whether the refinery-strike argument between Kyiv and Washington hardens into a condition or a concession.
Sources:
Source: 935thelloyd.com.

In short: another night of strikes on the grid and the ports, a Ukrainian advance in the east that is forcing Russia to spend its better units on defence, and an Oleshky ceasefire due Tuesday that both sides are already arguing about before it starts. Watch Tuesday for whether aid moves in Oleshky, and whether the refinery-strike argument between Kyiv and Washington hardens into a condition or a concession.

item.title: Tailscale SSH flaw ("Tailworm") — high severity, no CVE and no patch yet
item.description:
Security researchers from Cyberdione Labs report that an attacker who has already compromised one device on a network, and where SSH port forwarding is enabled in Tailscale SSH, can abuse connection handling to reach system sockets and read sensitive files or run commands with root privileges on other servers — without an extra password or key.
The issue was rated high severity in testing October 22–24 and identified in Tailscale version 1.104.2 and Headscale 0.29.5. Tailscale has acknowledged the report and is investigating with external experts.
If you run Tailscale SSH with port forwarding, watch for the patch and review which devices your access rules allow to connect. Source:
Source: thaicert.or.th.

item.title: "No strike today": Trump rules out a Sunday attack on Iran as Qatari mediators work Tehran
item.description:
President Donald Trump said Sunday there would be no American strike on Iran "today," closing out the weekend deadline he set himself on Saturday — while keeping the threat of renewed military action fully open. Asked by a reporter whether a US attack could come as soon as Sunday, Trump replied, according to The Jerusalem Post: "Would I tell you that? The answer is no. There will not be a strike today." Earlier Sunday, on Fox News' "Sunday Morning Futures," he framed the choice still ahead of him in his own terms, as CBS News reported: "Now, my question is, do I make a deal with them, or do I finish them off?"
The details matter because Saturday's version was deliberately vaguer. On Saturday Trump had said the US was "thinking about doing it, and maybe tomorrow," alongside the possibility of a "big, beautiful" agreement, and said he would not disclose his plans. Sunday's answer narrows that to a single day: no strike Sunday, no decision announced for the days after. The Jerusalem Post also reported the prevailing assessment in Washington is that Trump will hold off on a final decision until after the November 3 midterm elections — though US officials quoted by the paper described a joint US-Israeli strike as a question of "when," not "if." No new attack order or military timetable was announced Sunday.
Washington's argument, as Trump put it, is about permanence: the earlier B-2 operation was not enough to guarantee Iran never builds a nuclear weapon, so further action may be needed to "make it permanent." He also claimed the US controls the Strait of Hormuz and said it is monitoring Iran's Pickaxe Mountain nuclear site plus three other sites hit in earlier strikes, adding "there isn't much activity going on there." On Friday he had floated "another little Epic Fury," the name of the joint US-Israeli campaign against Iran that began in February.
Tehran's side of the argument is that it will not be moved by the threat, and that diplomacy is still alive but not on Washington's terms. Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Sunday that a resumption of war would not change Iran's positions, and that shipping through Hormuz would not return to its prewar arrangements. Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei said the window for diplomacy had not closed and messages were still passing through intermediaries, according to AP — but added that Washington kept demanding "complete surrender," which he said no Iranian would accept. And the diplomacy is not just messaging: Reuters reported, citing an official briefed on the situation, that Qatari mediators were in Tehran on Sunday as part of a US-coordinated effort to ease regional tensions, and Al Jazeera reported the same visit.
For ordinary people, the practical picture barely changed Sunday — and that is the point. The US State Department travel advisories updated earlier in the weekend for Saudi Arabia, Qatar, the UAE, Bahrain, Iraq, Lebanon and Israel still stand; the head of US Central Command, Admiral Brad Cooper, flew over the Strait of Hormuz on Sunday and said more than 3,000 commercial vessels had transited the waterway with US military support over the past six months, per AP. Gulf residents still face airport alerts and rerouted flights, and any fresh strike still risks another round of Hormuz disruption and higher fuel prices. The other shadow over the weekend is the intelligence warning reported Friday: US Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton warned Iran had "substantially increased efforts to target US personnel" abroad, with some plots at advanced stages, according to CBS News.
In short: Sunday's threatened strike did not happen, and Trump said so explicitly — but he ruled out one day, not the operation. With Qatari mediators in Tehran and both sides publicly insisting they want a deal on terms the other rejects, the next real decision point is after the November 3 midterms, not this weekend.
Sources:
Source: profilenews.com.

item.title: Yemen / Saudi: Sunday's barrage counted — 11 missiles over the south, and debris injuries for the first time this weekend
item.description:
The Institute for the Study of War's October 25 update puts numbers on Sunday's exchange: the Houthis have fired at least 12 missiles and two drones at Saudi Arabia since October 24, with Saudi air defences intercepting 11 missiles over southern Saudi Arabia, including Asir Province, on October 25.
A cruise missile aimed at Khamis Mushait was also intercepted. That corrects the morning picture of "no casualties linked": Saudi Civil Defense said debris from two intercepted missiles injured two people — a Saudi citizen and an Asian resident — and damaged three residential buildings and seven vehicles in Khamis Mushait and Ahad Rafidah.
The Houthis, for their part, said Saturday they carried out seven missile and drone operations against targets including King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, King Fahd International Airport in Dammam, Najran Airport, an airbase in Khamis Mushait, and Aramco refineries, pumping stations and the East-West pipeline, calling it retaliation for Saudi airstrikes on Yemen. Separately, Saudi Arabia's Interior Ministry warned that recording or circulating footage of interceptions or debris sites could bring legal action, and a fresh Riyadh alert was reported early Monday Saudi time.
Source:
Source: understandingwar.org.

item.title: Ukraine: a deep strike on a missile-parts plant, and the shopping-mall campaign's toll
item.description:
Ukrainian strikes reached the Energia plant in Yelets, in Russia's Lipetsk region, on Sunday afternoon, according to open-source tracking — the plant makes batteries and components for onboard electronics and missile guidance, linked by analysts to the Iskander-M, Iskander-K, Zircon and Kinzhal missiles and the Pantsir-S1 air-defence system.
That report is single-source OSINT, not a Ukrainian General Staff confirmation, so treat the damage assessment as unverified. Meanwhile the Institute for the Study of War's October 25 assessment confirms the other end of the exchange: Russian drone strikes on October 24–25 completely destroyed the Epicentr-K retail network's stores in four cities — Kharkiv, Zaporizhzhia, Vinnytsia and Poltava — and included a double-tap strike on emergency workers responding to an earlier hit in Kharkiv.
The same assessment, citing the Financial Times, reports that the threat of strikes has cut traffic through Ukrainian ports to fewer than 10 ships passing through Greater Odesa ports in September 2026, against roughly 400 in July. Source:
Source: understandingwar.org.

item.title: Sunday's deadline came and went — but a downed drone, a diplomat pullout, and a rearming carrier kept the Iran temperature high
item.description:
President Donald Trump said Saturday that the United States could strike Iran "maybe tomorrow" — meaning Sunday — or reach what he called a "big, beautiful" agreement, and Sunday passed with no US strike reported by late afternoon Central time. What did happen Sunday was a cluster of smaller moves that, taken together, point in the same direction: both sides are posturing hard while keeping a deal on the table, and neither has committed to either path.
The day's sharpest incident came early Sunday, when Iran's army said its air defences shot down a US LUCAS drone over Bandar Abbas, the southern port city near the Strait of Hormuz. Reuters carried the claim, citing Iran's semi-official Tasnim news agency. LUCAS — Low-cost Uncrewed Combat Attack System — is a cheap one-way attack drone, a US design modelled on Iran's Shahed-136, reportedly costing around $35,000 a unit. PressTV, Iran's state outlet, added that this was not the first LUCAS Iran says it has downed, pointing to another in July, and that the Revolutionary Guards claimed an MQ-9 Reaper downing over the strait earlier in the week. No US confirmation of Sunday's shootdown had appeared in the reporting by this evening, and Iranian accounts themselves differed on the location, with some pointing to the Jask coastal area rather than Bandar Abbas — so treat the shootdown as an Iranian claim carried by Reuters, not an independently verified event.
Trump's own words are the second strand. Asked Saturday in Florida how far along a possible attack was, he said, according to Middle East Eye and Al Jazeera's live coverage: "Do you really think I'd tell you that. Maybe tomorrow... There's a possibility I will. There's also a possibility we'll have a nice, big, beautiful agreement. They want to make a deal, but the problem is, will they hold the deal?" That directly undercuts his October 8 pledge not to attack Iran before the November 3 midterms — a reversal his critics noted and his supporters framed as keeping Tehran guessing. US Ambassador to Turkey Tom Barrack went further on Friday, telling podcaster Mario Nawfal that a strike "this weekend" was possible, while Trump himself responded that he knew nothing about Barrack's remark — a public split inside the administration's messaging.
The third strand is quieter but arguably more telling: preparation. CNN reported Friday, citing multiple sources and a State Department official, that the US is quietly moving some diplomats and family members out of posts in Lebanon, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar and Jordan as concern grows over further regional escalation. Axios reported an October 23 intelligence memorandum to Secretary of State Marco Rubio, confirmed by a US official to the Jerusalem Post, warning that Iran has substantially increased efforts to target American personnel, with some plots at advanced stages. And the Wall Street Journal reported from aboard the USS George Washington on Sunday that the carrier is rearming in preparation for possible strikes on Iran — a report carried in summary form, with no figures on munitions or any timeline, so it reads as readiness signalling rather than a strike order.
Iran's side of the argument, meanwhile, is that Washington derailed the talks. President Masoud Pezeshkian said on state television that negotiations over an interim agreement were under way before "the cowards (Americans) messed everything up," while still saying Iran should go and conclude a deal. Iran's armed forces chief, Major General Ali Abdollahi, said Saturday that US warships would not be allowed back into the Persian Gulf under any circumstances. And an IRGC-affiliated outlet on Sunday rejected reports that Tehran had offered, via a Pakistani mediator, to reopen the Strait of Hormuz in exchange for lifting the US naval blockade — a reminder that even the supposed diplomatic off-ramps are disputed. Regional voices weighed in against fresh strikes: Egypt, Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan warned that renewed attacks would deepen regional instability, according to Arab News and the Times of Israel, while European and Middle Eastern ministers urged diplomacy instead.
For ordinary people, the stakes are the ones already visible in their bills and travel plans: any fresh strike risks another round of Hormuz disruption and higher fuel prices, Gulf governments are already warning their own citizens and visitors, and the US State Department has updated travel advisories for Saudi Arabia, Qatar, the UAE, Bahrain, Iraq, Lebanon and Israel, citing potential Houthi threats. None of that is abstract for Gulf residents — it is airport alerts, rerouted flights and a risk premium on everything shipped through the strait.
In short: Sunday's threatened strike did not materialise, but the ingredients for one — a claimed drone shootdown, an intelligence warning about targeting US personnel, diplomats quietly leaving posts, and a carrier rearming — all moved in the same 48 hours, while both Trump and Pezeshkian kept talking about a deal neither side seems able to close.

item.title: Ukraine: no new daytime barrage — but a new wrinkle in the Starlink argument
item.description:
No major new daytime strike wave was reported in Ukraine on Sunday beyond the overnight barrage already covered in the morning brief.
The one new detail comes from CNN's Starlink reporting: Trump said he asked Elon Musk to lift restrictions on Kyiv's military-grade Starlink/Starshield service, while Trump and his top officials denied making the call to throttle it in the first place — and Musk said the administration was behind the ban in a social media post last week. Ukraine's defence ministry says restored speeds above 400 km/h are now being recorded.
In other words, all three parties now agree speeds are back, but nobody agrees on who restricted them or why — the same dispute the morning brief flagged, now with each side's version on the record. Watch Tuesday, October 27, for the Oleshky local ceasefire.

item.title: Yemen / Saudi: Reuters confirms Sunday's interceptions; US travel advice updated
item.description:
Reuters confirmed Sunday afternoon that Saudi Arabia intercepted drones and missiles over Riyadh and southern areas, with civil defence alerts issued for Riyadh, Abha and Khamis Mushait before the all-clear — an independent wire confirmation of the coalition interception claims in the morning brief, rather than new casualty claims.
No new Saudi or Houthi casualty figures surfaced Sunday beyond those already reported. Separately, the US State Department updated travel advisories for Saudi Arabia, Qatar, the UAE, Bahrain, Iraq, Lebanon and Israel, citing potential Houthi threats — the practical consequence for travellers of a missile campaign that has now run for over two weeks.
Riyadh's Terminals 1 and 2, reopened Sunday morning, remain the test case for whether civilian aviation can operate through it.

item.title: Sweet Security Research Identifies Go Implementation of Node2Shell Vulnerability, Expanding Attack Surface to Major HTTP Frameworks
item.description:
The Brotli flaw behind Node2Shell is not C-only: Sweet Security found a parallel fix pushed to Go's Brotli library on October 23, confirming the same vulnerability class in Go. That pulls Traefik (direct dependency, Compress middleware), Fiber (via fasthttp) and Iris into scope — combined adoption over 130,000 GitHub stars, Traefik alone over a billion Docker pulls. Sweet Security cautions that dependency presence alone does not prove exploitability — version, encoder-vs-decoder use and configuration matter — but says Go HTTP services decoding client-controlled Brotli input should be inventoried now. This extends the Node.js Brotli fixes already reported October 22; it is not a new KEV entry. Source: GlobeNewswire / Sweet Security.
Watch Monday: CISA KEV federal patch deadlines land October 26 for Nextcloud Collabora (CVE-2026-110447) and Arista VeloCloud (CVE-2026-114625), both already reported and actively exploited.
Source: globenewswire.com.

item.title: A night of drones on both sides — and a public fight over Starlink
item.description:
Russia fired 153 Shahed-type drones at Ukraine overnight into Sunday, including 92 faster jet-powered variants, along with low-cost Banderol cruise missiles, according to Ukraine's Air Force as reported by the Kyiv Independent. Ukraine said it neutralized 119 of the 153 drones, with debris and impacts recorded at 15 locations. The human toll is still being reconciled across reports: the Kyiv Independent-based tally puts 8 people killed and 51 wounded across Ukraine over the past day, while other Sunday reports cite at least 4 killed and 32 injured. A drone hit a residential building in Vinnytsia, injuring six; in Synelnykove, Dnipropetrovsk region, a strike on an apartment building killed four people, including victims who later died in hospital, and injured at least 13, including an 11-year-old girl. In Kharkiv, Russian forces first struck a home-improvement hypermarket, then hit the emergency crews who arrived — a double-tap strike that injured first responders and destroyed a fire engine tanker.
Russia reported its own casualties from Ukrainian strikes. Belgorod's governor said an overnight Ukrainian drone attack on the city killed two people and injured 13, damaging 30 apartment blocks, and another person was killed near Shebekino. In Bryansk region, a drone attack on a minibus belonging to an agricultural enterprise killed two and seriously injured two more. Russia's Defence Ministry said its forces struck Ukrainian logistics centres, port infrastructure and a dry-cargo vessel it claimed was carrying supplies for Ukraine's armed forces near Chornomorsk, and claimed 532 Ukrainian drones were intercepted over 25 Russian regions overnight. Reuters noted it could not independently verify the ministry's claims, and the same caveat applies to both sides' tallies.
The two sides also fought publicly over the satellite link Ukrainian forces depend on. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk wrote on X that Ukraine's military violated Starlink's terms of service by using the civilian service for offensive drone strikes to "kill people," and said that "loophole was closed last week" — a statement that, if it refers to the speed restrictions Ukrainian officials complained about for weeks, would explain them. Ukrainian presidential adviser Serhiy Beskrestnov pushed back, saying commercial Starlink terminals are technically incapable of supporting long-range strikes because of active speed restrictions. Meanwhile Kyiv says Starlink/Starshield access has been restored to full speeds, improving drone command-and-control — a claim that sits uneasily next to Musk's post, and neither side has fully explained the sequence.
President Zelensky used the overnight toll to press his case for air defence. In a Sunday post he said Russia launched around 1,600 guided aerial bombs, 48 missiles and nearly 2,300 attack drones over the past week, hitting a thermal power plant, substations, coal mines, grain storage, shopping malls and a postal logistics hub across nine regions. "This is how Russia responds to diplomacy and deisolation," he wrote, urging European partners to unblock already-approved Patriot interceptor deliveries and keep supporting Ukrainian combat aviation against jet-powered Shaheds.
For ordinary Ukrainians, the pattern is now the war itself: apartment blocks, shops and warehouses hit nightly, emergency crews targeted while responding, and winter approaching with the power grid already under strain. The Oleshky local ceasefire — the one agreed pause in weeks — is still set for Tuesday, October 27, but nothing in the overnight exchange suggests the wider war is slowing for it.
In short: both sides traded heavy drone strikes overnight with civilians killed on both sides of the border, the casualty counts differ by outlet and remain unverified, and the Starlink dispute has moved from quiet restrictions into an open argument between Musk and Kyiv over what the system may be used for.
Sources:
Source: americastrikes.com.

item.title: Riyadh airport reopens its first terminals as the coalition says it stopped 10 missiles
item.description:
King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh reopened Terminals 1 and 2 on Sunday, the first sign of normal operations returning after two weeks in which the airport was repeatedly targeted — including the October 10 strike that killed 13 people and wounded more than 300. The Houthis immediately called the reopened airport a "military target" and warned it is not safe for airlines, employees or travellers, renewing the evacuation warning they have issued since the airport campaign began.
The reopening came under fire. The Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted a ballistic missile and a drone over Riyadh overnight, destroyed a Houthi cruise missile aimed at Khamis Mushait on Sunday morning, and shortly before noon said it had intercepted and destroyed ten Houthi ballistic missiles aimed at the Southern Region. No casualties were linked to the latest interceptions in coalition statements, and there was no independent confirmation of damage from the Houthi side's claims. The Houthis had claimed seven operations on Saturday, including strikes on Riyadh and Dammam airports, Yanbu Aramco facilities, the Rabigh refinery and the East-West pipeline — claims Saudi authorities have not confirmed for the oil sites.
The two narratives have barely moved all month, and that is the story: the coalition reports interceptions and counts no hits; the Houthis claim hits on airports and energy sites and count no need for Saudi confirmation. What changed Sunday is the airport itself — Riyadh is testing whether partial reopening is sustainable while missiles are still being fired at it, and the Houthis are testing whether they can keep that bet from paying off. Egypt's parliament is due to resume its session on Saudi defence authorisation on Monday, October 26, a vote that could formalise more regional backing for the coalition.
For travellers and for the region's economy, the stakes are concrete: Riyadh's airport is the kingdom's main gateway, its closure has already forced airlines to suspend or reroute Gulf services for weeks, and every intercepted missile over the capital keeps the risk premium on Gulf aviation and shipping where it is. If Terminals 1 and 2 stay open through the week, that is a genuine de-escalation signal; if a missile gets through, the closure returns overnight.
In short: Riyadh reopened part of its airport under fire, the coalition says it stopped 11 missiles and drones in a single day, the Houthis say the airport remains a target — and the question of whether civilian aviation can operate through a missile campaign is now being answered in real time.
Sources:
Source: defenseandtech.com.

item.title: Iran / US: post-midterm strike planning reported, no decision confirmed
item.description:
CNN and the New York Times have reported, over October 21–25, that US officials have discussed a short but intense campaign against Iran after the November 3 midterms — roughly three days of strikes on nuclear facilities, energy infrastructure and missile and drone arsenals, coordinated with Israel — while President Trump has publicly pledged not to attack Iran before the midterms and has not confirmed any final decision.
Trump said Saturday the US could take further military action against Iran or reach a deal, without specifying timing. Treat this as reported planning, not a decision: the White House has said it does not comment on military plans "that may or may not exist," and Trump has repeatedly vetoed proposals for a return to major combat this year.
Sources:
Source: suaragarut.id.

item.title: Hormuz shipping costs: tracker puts freight plus war-risk surcharges above $40 a barrel
item.description:
A daily Hormuz tracker refreshed October 25 assesses the threat index as critical and puts combined freight and war-risk insurance surcharges above $40 per barrel on Gulf routes, with operators shifting to ship-to-ship transfers off Oman to bypass the strait.
October remains the worst month on record for shipping attacks in the corridor (28 attacks, per the Washington Institute). This is a tracker estimate, not an official figure, and the underlying mine claims for two supertankers remain unverified by any maritime authority.
Source:
Source: regionalert.com.

item.title: Keystone wallet breach: customer names and shipping addresses exposed
item.description:
Hardware wallet maker Keystone said unauthorized access to its website exposed customer contact and shipping information.
The company says private keys, recovery phrases and payment details were not compromised — so the risk here is phishing and physical-targeting scams using the leaked contact details, not drained wallets. Keystone urged customers to ignore unexpected messages claiming to be from the company and never enter recovery phrases into unfamiliar devices.
Source:
Source: abijita.com.

item.title: CVE-2026-116068: Dokploy cross-organization authorization bypass, CVSS 8.8

item.title: Houthis open a second front in Aden as Saudi strikes kill up to 16 in Yemen
item.description:
The Houthis struck Yemen's interim capital Aden on Saturday while also firing at targets across Saudi Arabia, opening a second front against the Saudi-backed government on its own territory. Yemen's Interior Ministry said two missiles hit the coast guard headquarters inside the ministry's compound and a third struck a coast guard building in the Tawahi district, according to the state-run Saba news agency. Separately, Yemen's Transport Ministry said two ballistic missiles hit Aden International Airport, calling it the "fourth such attack this month" and warning of "a threat to the safety of civil aviation." No casualties were reported in Aden, and an Anadolu Agency correspondent heard three explosions across the city.
The two sides describe the Aden strikes differently, and the gap matters. Houthi spokesman Yahya Saree said his forces targeted "Saudi enemy concentrations" at the al-Nasr camp and a naval base in Aden, naming a Saudi brigadier general he said oversaw them. Saree did not mention the airport; the government did not mention al-Nasr camp. Whether they are describing the same impacts under different names or separate strikes is unclear. What is clear is the intent: the Houthis are framing Aden not as Yemen's capital under attack but as a Saudi forward base, while the government treats the coast guard — a force Saudi Arabia has funded and equipped to patrol the Red Sea approach — as its own.
On the Saudi side, the coalition confirmed intercepting three ballistic missiles aimed at Riyadh, Yanbu and Taif, plus a drone in the Eastern Province, and debris fell in Mecca, Jeddah, Taif and Rabigh. Saree claimed far more — eight sites including the Yanbu Aramco facility, the Rabigh refinery, the East-West pipeline, Dammam and Najran airports and Khamis Mushait air base — but Saudi authorities confirmed none of the oil-site hits. The pattern of the last two weeks held: Houthi claims run well ahead of what Riyadh confirms.
The human cost on the other side of the exchange came from Houthi-run Al-Masirah, relayed by AFP: Saudi strikes killed 11 in Sanaa — four in a house and six women and a child at a cement factory's workers' housing — plus five more in a family home in Hodeida, for a reported total of 16. Saudi Arabia has not commented on civilian casualties in Yemen, and independent verification inside Houthi-held territory is effectively impossible, so those figures are one side's account, not confirmed tolls. The Aden strikes follow a pattern this month: the presidential palace on October 15 (5 killed, 16 wounded) and a military coordination site near the airport on October 21, now the coast guard command — each attack picking off a different node of the Saudi-backed government's infrastructure.
For ordinary people, the stakes are aviation and everyday safety: a fourth missile attack this month on Aden's only functioning commercial airport, debris falling across Saudi Arabia's western seaboard including Mecca and Jeddah, and another round of civilian deaths in Sanaa and Hodeida. The GCC secretary-general called the attacks on Saudi Arabia "heinous," but there has been no comparable UN Security Council statement on the Aden strikes.
In short: the Houthis are now fighting on two fronts in a single day — Saudi cities from the south and the Saudi-backed government in Aden from the north — and the war's civilian toll is rising on both sides of the exchange, with the claims on each side still unverified where it matters most.
Sources:
Source: houseofsaud.com.

item.title: Oleshky ceasefire firms up for October 27 — and Starlink is back, Ukrainian officials say
item.description:
The local ceasefire both sides agreed to on Friday now has a converging start date, and a second long-running friction point appears to have eased. Kyiv and Moscow both say their forces will stop firing around the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky from October 27 — Russia's General Gerasimov put it at 4 a.m. Moscow time, Ukraine's ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets at 3 a.m. Kyiv time, the same moment — to let aid in and civilians out. The White House statement still says October 29, a discrepancy that has not been resolved, but the two armies that would actually have to hold fire now agree on the 27th. Ukraine's top negotiator says the ceasefire will cover the wider Kherson region and neighbouring areas needed for the operation, and last several days.
The deal was brokered with US First Lady Melania Trump as what her office called the "exclusive intermediary," and the Kremlin credited her with a "significant contribution." Civilian, non-military officials from both countries are to visit residents at home to assess needs, and those who want to leave will be taken to Russia or to Ukraine, their choice. Around 1,700 civilians remain in Oleshky, down from 24,000 before the war, and conditions are dire: mined roads, limited electricity, and, according to a Nobel Peace Prize-winning Ukrainian activist cited by CNN, people eating grass, with the last official food delivery in May. Pope Leo also raised the town with both Putin and Zelensky in the past week.
Separately, the Institute for the Study of War's October 24 assessment says Ukrainian officials are confirming the resumption of unrestricted access to Starlink and Starshield — the satellite system Ukrainian forces rely on for communications and missile warning — after weeks of speed restrictions that Kyiv said disrupted military operations. That is a sharp change from Friday, when Ukrainian officials said the curbs were still in place despite President Trump's claim they had been lifted. No official explanation for the restrictions, or their lifting, has been given.
On the wider war, the diplomatic track also moved: Zelensky said negotiators from Ukraine, Russia and the US agreed to technical-level talks in the first half of November in Abu Dhabi, though a US official later said Abu Dhabi or Switzerland within a couple of weeks. Zelensky said he hopes a leaders' meeting follows, but cautioned that much depends on Russia — a similar meeting expected this month never happened, and Moscow still demands all of Donbas, including territory it does not control, which Kyiv rejects.
For ordinary Ukrainians, the Oleshky deal is narrow — one town, a few days — but it is the first agreed pause either side has confirmed in weeks, and restored Starlink access matters far beyond it: it affects how Ukrainian forces communicate, coordinate and receive warning of incoming missiles. The November talks are the real test of whether a humanitarian opening becomes anything bigger.
In short: both armies now agree the Oleshky guns fall silent October 27, Starlink restrictions appear lifted, and three-way talks are set for early November — modest steps, but the first ones in the same direction in weeks.
Sources:
Source: reuters.com.

item.title: Oil at $117: the US taps its emergency reserve as Hormuz claims go unverified
item.description:
Brent crude briefly topped $117 a barrel on Friday — its highest since the war involving Iran began — and settled at $116.72, with WTI at $103.27, as the Strait of Hormuz shipping crisis kept tightening. The US Department of Energy on Friday authorized an emergency exchange of up to 400,000 barrels from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve for Phillips 66's Lake Charles refinery in Louisiana, to offset a crude delivery disruption. Reuters notes the reserve is already at its lowest since 1982 after the releases tied to the Iran war, and this draw, like the 4-million-barrel hurricane exchange earlier in October, is a loan: Phillips 66 must return more barrels than it borrows.
The price spike is being driven by claims that remain unverified. Iran's Revolutionary Guard said two supertankers carrying more than 4.5 million barrels combined struck naval mines on what Tehran calls an unauthorized southern route, with crews abandoning both vessels — a claim carried by Iranian state media and several regional outlets but confirmed by no maritime authority. President Trump dismissed the claims on Thursday as fabricated to lift oil prices before the November 3 midterms, saying more oil is moving through Hormuz than before the war. Independent monitors split the difference: IMF PortWatch recorded just 4 transits on October 18 against a pre-crisis baseline of 85 per day, while Kpler put total oil flows for the week ending October 18 at 24.5 million barrels per day — roughly pre-war levels, rerouted rather than stopped.
October is already the worst month on record for attacks on commercial shipping in and around the strait, per MarineLink and Reuters, with 28 attacks in the month and 113 since February 28. An Iranian envoy also said Iran remains open to talks with the US under a Pakistan-brokered deal, according to AP — a diplomatic thread running alongside the military one.
For ordinary people, this is already a fuel-price story: diesel prices in Europe have jumped sharply, US fuel markets are leaning on an emergency reserve at 1980s lows, and every unverified mine claim moves the pump price regardless of whether a ship actually sank. The gap between what Tehran claims, what Washington denies, and what shippers can confirm is itself now a market force.
In short: oil is at wartime highs, the US is lending from a depleted emergency stockpile, and the Hormuz shipping war is being fought as much through claims and counterclaims as through actual strikes — watch whether any independent authority confirms a vessel loss, which would be the next real escalation.
Sources:
Source: reuters.com.

item.title: Microduck — a tiny open-source robot duck that walks with reinforcement learning
item.description:
Pollen Robotics' Microduck is a 25 cm, 800 g biped driven by a 50 Hz control loop over 15 servos, with policies trained in simulation (MuJoCo/PPO) and exported to ONNX.
It walks, rolls, picks things up and gets back up when knocked over. The software is Rust, Apache-2.0, and it was trending on GitHub with ~11,000 stars.
Source:
Source: digisoulhub.com.

item.title: Capcom breach: 11.7 million CAPCOM ID emails exposed (catch-up, disclosed October 22)
item.description:
Capcom confirmed unauthorized third-party access to its CAPCOM ID membership service, exposing email addresses plus account creation date, last login, login count and last-login IP for 11,774,247 accounts.
For 43 accounts, birth dates, gender, country and nicknames were also exposed, and 196 accounts had passwords changed without authorization (since reset). No credit card data was involved.
Capcom detected the intrusion October 19 and reported it to Osaka police and Japan's privacy regulator October 21. The real risk now is phishing using the leaked emails.
Sources:
Source: beebom.com.

item.title: Electrum 4.8.3 patches a flaw that let rogue servers steal Bitcoin
item.description:
A malicious server could swap a user's payment for a fraudulent one, and when the user bumped the fee (RBF), they signed the theft themselves.
One user reported a loss; every version before 4.8.3 is affected. Update at electrum.org.

item.title: Houthis claim a coast-to-coast strike wave; Saudis report intercepts over Taif and Yanbu, and Sanaa reports 11 dead in retaliation strikes
item.description:
The Saturday fighting in the Saudi–Houthi war widened from the capital to the Red Sea coast. In a statement carried by the Houthi-run Saba news agency at about 7 PM local time, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree claimed seven missile and drone operations: King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, an Aramco facility in Yanbu, the Rabigh refinery, pumping stations and the East-West crude pipeline, King Fahd International Airport in Dammam, Najran airport, and the air base at Khamis Mushait. Saree claimed every target was hit and that air traffic at Dammam was disrupted. None of that has been independently verified, and Saudi authorities had not confirmed any hits on oil sites at the time of writing, according to Defense and Tech's summary of the day's statements.
What the coalition does confirm is a second wave of intercepts after the morning's Riyadh missile, which was covered in the morning brief. Later Saturday, the coalition said it destroyed two ballistic missiles fired toward Taif and Yanbu, and Saudi Civil Defence briefly issued alerts for Taif, Yanbu, Mecca and Jeddah, lifting them about ten minutes later, Reuters reports via Defense and Tech. Civil Defence said debris from the intercepted missiles fell in Wadi al-Mughammas in Mecca, Jeddah's al-Nuzha district, Wadi Jalil in Taif, and the Mastoura area of Rabigh governorate. No casualties were mentioned in the Civil Defence statement, and it did not address the Houthi claims about Aramco, the pipeline, or the Rabigh refinery.
The two sides tell very different stories about the retaliation. Saree said the strikes were retaliation for what he described as 100 Saudi air strikes on Sanaa and other Houthi-held areas in the previous 24 hours. The Houthi-run Health Ministry in Sanaa said Saudi aircraft hit a house in the capital's Asr area, killing three people and injuring three, and hit workers' housing at a cement factory in Hamdan district, killing eight people — including three women and four children — and injuring 15. Defense and Tech notes it had not seen a coalition statement on those reports. Separately, Yemen's internationally recognised government said three Houthi ballistic missiles hit coast guard sites in Aden, Reuters reports.
Why Yanbu and Rabigh matter: Yanbu, on the Red Sea, is the western end of Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline, which lets the kingdom export crude without sending it through the Strait of Hormuz. Rabigh, on the same coast north of Jeddah, hosts a large refining complex. Any confirmed damage there would matter well beyond Saudi Arabia — which is exactly why the gap between the Houthi claim and the Saudi account matters, and why neither should be taken as confirmed yet. One earlier claim did gain partial Saudi confirmation Saturday: on Thursday, Oct 22, the Houthis claimed attacks on the defence ministry in Riyadh, Aramco facilities in Yanbu, and Dammam airport, and Saudi authorities said two people were killed in Dammam but did not confirm the other two claims, according to Reuters.
In short: Saturday's war of claims stretched from Riyadh to the Red Sea coast, with confirmed intercepts over Taif and Yanbu, unconfirmed Houthi claims of hits on Yanbu, Rabigh and the East-West pipeline, and 11 reported dead in Sanaa from Saudi retaliation strikes. Watch for any Saudi confirmation or denial on the oil sites, and any independent evidence of damage at Yanbu or Rabigh.
Sources:
Source: defenseandtech.com.

item.title: Crimea's blackout is now a rationing regime — power and water restricted, trolleybuses halted, no restoration timeline
item.description:
Saturday brought the first official picture of how bad the Crimea blackout is, and it is worse than a one-night outage. Sergei Aksyonov, the Moscow-installed head of Crimea, said restrictions on electricity and water are now in force across the peninsula after what he called an accident on the main power lines outside Crimea caused by a drone attack. Sevastopol's Russian-installed governor, Mikhail Razvozhaev, said only about 40% of the city's basic mobile-communication base stations are working, trolleybus service has been suspended, and water has been supplied at reduced pressure in parts of Sevastopol's Leninsky district since 9 AM Saturday, with water trucks organised for residents. Social facilities are running on backup power, and Razvozhaev said generator reserves last about four hours before mobile crews recharge them. Kyiv24 reports the timeline for full restoration is currently unknown.
The details behind the blackout are still contested. Monitoring channel Crimean Wind reported a fire at the Taman substation in Russia's Krasnodar Krai, through which all four lines of the Kerch Strait energy bridge run, and NASA FIRMS satellite imagery indicated damage there, according to earlier reporting. Nightwatch's Saturday intelligence summary says Russia's Energy Ministry confirmed new power disruption affecting consumers in occupied Crimea and occupied parts of Kherson, Zaporizhzhia, Donetsk and Luhansk oblasts, but cautions that the Taman fire is corroborated while its connection to the full outage footprint and the extent of physical damage remain unresolved. The Kyiv Independent could not independently verify the extent of the blackouts, and Ukrainian military officials have not commented. For ordinary people, the distinction matters less than the rationing: rolling outages, patchy mobile service, suspended electric transport, and reduced water pressure are now the daily reality until the grid is repaired.
Elsewhere in Ukraine on Saturday, Ukrainian officials said Russian drone and missile strikes across eastern Ukraine killed at least five people, according to Storysh, and a Russian strike on Chernihiv set a disused building ablaze and injured two people, EGazette reports. In Russia, Nightwatch notes imagery supporting fires after UAV activity over Omsk, but says identification of the affected facilities remains preliminary.
In short: Crimea has gone from blackout to rationing — power, water, mobile service and trolleybuses all restricted, with no restoration date — while the exact damage at the Taman substation and its link to the full outage remain unverified. Watch for restoration claims versus renewed blackouts in Simferopol, Yalta and Alushta, which already flickered once after initial restoration claims.
Sources:
Source: kyiv24.com.
item.content:encoded:
Saturday brought the first official picture of how bad the Crimea blackout is, and it is worse than a one-night outage. Sergei Aksyonov, the Moscow-installed head of Crimea, said restrictions on electricity and water are now in force across the peninsula after what he called an accident on the main power lines outside Crimea caused by a drone attack. Sevastopol's Russian-installed governor, Mikhail Razvozhaev, said only about 40% of the city's basic mobile-communication base stations are working, trolleybus service has been suspended, and water has been supplied at reduced pressure in parts of Sevastopol's Leninsky district since 9 AM Saturday, with water trucks organised for residents. item.title: Oleshky — new details on the Oct 27 deal:
item.description:
Reuters, CNN and The Times have now filled in the diplomacy behind the local ceasefire reported in the morning brief.
The deal was brokered with US First Lady Melania Trump acting as what her office calls the "exclusive intermediary," working directly with Ukrainian and Russian leadership; she said Oleshky's remaining 1,700–2,000 residents are mostly elderly in urgent need of medicine, food and clean water, with 30–50 children also thought to be in the town, and that residents who evacuate will get transport to their preferred destination — "some will want to go to Russia, and some to Ukraine." Newsmax says it was granted exclusive TV access to document the operation.
On the wider war, Zelensky said technical-level talks with Russia and the US are set for the first half of November in Abu Dhabi, while a US official later said the next round could be in Abu Dhabi or Switzerland within a couple of weeks. The Oct 27 vs Oct 29 start-date dispute flagged in the morning brief is still unresolved.
Sources:
Source: reuters.com.

item.title: Hormuz — the oil paradox:
item.description:
Total oil flows actually reached 24.5 million barrels per day in the week ending Oct 18 — slightly above the 24.4 million pre-war average from Feb 22 — according to Kpler data reported by TuzaraPost, because Gulf producers rerouted exports around the strait via the Red Sea and other alternatives.
But traffic through the strait itself is a fraction of normal: about 20 ships a day versus 100+ before the war, with many running dark (transponders off). US Central Command's claim of about 400 merchant transits in the preceding week is far higher than Kpler's count — the gap itself is a measure of how murky the strait picture is.
The IRGC says the strait is closed; CENTCOM says it is open; both can be half-right at once when "open" means a trickle of dark ships. Source:
Source: tuzarapost.substack.com.

item.title: iPhone Duo launch day: lines returned, walk-ins sold out within hours, resales hit $10,000 — and Apple briefly retook the world's most-valuable crown
item.description:
Apple's first foldable had the kind of launch day the iPhone hasn't seen in years. MacRumors reports queues of dozens to hundreds of people at Apple Stores worldwide on Friday, with some lining up a day or two early; Apple's CEO John Ternus and retail chief Deirdre O'Brien greeted customers in Austin, while marketing chief Greg Joswiak did the same at Fifth Avenue in New York, where video showed a massive queue as early as 4:15 AM. Apple had warned walk-in stock would be "limited," and it was: the NY Post reports Fifth Avenue was out of stock for walk-ins by around 10 AM, King of Prussia (Pennsylvania) sold out shortly after 8 AM, and other stores followed within hours. The scarcity fed instant resale markups — eBay listings up to $10,000 for a 2TB Night Sky model against a $3,199 purchase price, and a Craigslist listing at $7,999, per the NY Post.
The launch day also briefly reshuffled the market-cap leaderboard. 9to5Mac reports Apple traded above $351 on Friday, a new intraday record, reaching a market value around $5.12 trillion and retaking the title of world's most valuable company from Nvidia. The lead did not clearly hold: one tracker had Nvidia back ahead by roughly $20 billion at the close, and Ainvest notes the flip was driven mostly by Nvidia's 4.4% fall on Oct 22 in a broad AI-stock sell-off rather than by Duo sales alone — Apple rose only about 1% to its record close. For buyers, the practical takeaway is simpler than the market-cap drama: Duo demand is real, walk-in supply is thin, and Apple had pointed shoppers to a Saturday check of the Apple Store app for pickup availability.
In short: the Duo's launch day combined genuine demand (lines, same-day sellouts) with scalper markups up to 3x retail, and a market-cap crown that Apple grabbed intraday and may not have kept at the close. Watch for restock timing and whether the hinge-crease reports from early owners turn into a real defect pattern.
Sources:
Source: macrumors.com.

item.title: NVIDIA OpenShell — the agent sandbox runtime, trending:
item.description:
OpenShell, Nvidia's open-source runtime for running AI agents safely, hit GitHub trending on Saturday with about 18.7k stars.
It is Apache-2.0, written in Rust, latest release v0.1.5 (Oct 20). Each agent runs in its own kernel-enforced sandbox, every network connection passes a policy check before leaving the sandbox, agents never see real credentials (OpenShell injects them only into requests to approved endpoints), and risky policy changes get flagged by formal verification before a human approves them.
Why it matters: it is the practical answer to "let the agent do things, but not everything" — the same OpenShell name appeared in Nvidia's GTC Berlin reference architecture this week, but this is the runtime itself gaining traction. Sources:
Source: digisoulhub.com.

item.title: PHP2Shell — first confirmed break-in, Palo Alto affected, patch lag now the story:
item.description:
The flaw is no longer just a warning. Palo Alto Networks' Unit 42 reports the first confirmed PHP2Shell compromise, at a European government body, carried out with an AI attack agent, according to Carthage Electronics' Oct 24 threat brief.
Palo Alto confirmed on Oct 24 that the flaws affect its PAN-OS and Panorama management interfaces (product impact rated 8.7, below the underlying PHP 9.2), with no malicious exploitation against its own products known so far — fixed hotfixes are dated Oct 26 (11.1.16-h4) and Oct 28 (12.2.4-h1), with Panorama versions still to be confirmed; until then, restrict management-interface access to trusted addresses only. Meanwhile the patch lag is measurable: more than 21,000 Danish websites still lacked PHP security updates as of Saturday, per Danish industry reporting via NordiskPost, with Denmark's Aula school platform and the Danish Meteorological Institute among precautionary shutdowns (Norway and Finland took similar precautions), and South Africa's Presidency website remained offline as a precaution, with a spokesperson telling Reuters there was no indication of a breach.
Cloudflare's Matthew Prince said exploitation attempts on Cloudflare's network rose from thousands before disclosure to millions after. Most of what researchers see is still scanning, not confirmed mass break-ins — but the first confirmed compromise means the window for "we'll patch Monday" is closing.
Sources:
Source: carthageelectronics.com.

item.title: HPE Aruba — eight CVSS 10.0 flaws, patch this weekend if you run Aruba gear:
item.description:
HPE's advisory HPESBNW05162 (Oct 22) patches 72 vulnerabilities in the ArubaOS systems running wireless networks, and eight carry the maximum CVSS score of 10.0 — authentication bypasses, command injection, SQL injection and buffer overflows letting an unauthenticated attacker run commands on AOS-8 and AOS-10 Mobility Conductors, Controllers, Gateways and Access Points, several via the PAPI access-point management protocol on UDP port 8211.
HPE says it is not aware of exploit code or attacks. Fixed releases: AOS-10 10.8.1.2, 10.7.2.7, 10.4.1.14 and AOS-8 8.13.3.1, 8.10.0.24.
Aruba gear sits in a lot of schools, clinics, warehouses and offices, so this is a weekend-planning item, not a Monday item. Source:
Source: carthageelectronics.com.

item.title: Quest Diagnostics breach confirmed — patient records accessed, scope still unknown:
item.description:
Quest told the SEC (8-K filed Oct 22) that it learned on Oct 21 of unauthorised access to its Quanum Lab Services Manager platform, used by healthcare clients to order lab tests and retrieve results.
Its Oct 23 security notice confirmed protected health information and personally identifiable information were involved, including "personal information and patient records," but the company has not disclosed how many patients are affected, which data types were taken, or when the intrusion began. Clinics relying on Quanum LSM are being told to place orders on paper forms or through Quanum eLabs, per BleepingComputer reporting.
If your doctor sends samples to Quest, this is one to watch — not a reason to panic, but a reason to watch insurance statements and unexpected messages. Sources:
Source: techycluster.com.
